quote: On the other hand, we are never going back to Newtonian mechanics. The ratchet of science turns, but it does not turn in reverse. There are cases in scientific history where a theory suffered a wound or two, and then bounced back; but when a theory takes as many arrows through the chest as Newtonian mechanics, it stays dead.
content: Theories come back from the dead often enough that the ratchet is a poor metaphor. Atomism was dead from Aristotle to Dalton; the corpuscular theory of light was killed by Young and Fresnel and revived as the photon; continental drift was rejected for forty years and revived as plate tectonics; the steady expansion of the universe was replaced by deceleration and then by acceleration; and Newtonian mechanics itself did not die, since it survives as the low-velocity limit of relativity and is the theory the essay’s artillery gunner correctly uses. The essay’s next sentence needs the ratchet, because it wants “to perdition with any past civilizations that disagreed” to be safe. But the ratchet is exactly what the pessimistic meta-induction denies, and the essay’s own case, general relativity, is one it concedes “some future physicist may overturn.” What actually does not reverse is the accumulation of empirical constraints: any successor to Newton has to reproduce Newton where Newton worked. That is a fact about data, not about theories, and it is what the essay should have said.

quote: If it were possible to build and run a chromodynamic model of the 747, it would yield accurate predictions. Better predictions than the aerodynamic model, in fact.
content: Three things are wrong with this in-principle claim. The Standard Model does not contain gravity, and a 747 in flight is an object on which gravity is the load being balanced, so the “chromodynamic model” is not a model of the aircraft. More seriously, the fundamental model would predict the flight only for a fully specified initial microstate, which is not available and, in a chaotic fluid, not usable; the aerodynamic model predicts robust quantities, lift as a function of angle of attack, that the fundamental model can reproduce only by averaging over microstates, and the averaging reintroduces the higher-level variables (Batterman (2000) on why universal behaviour is explained asymptotically and not from the fundamental theory alone). Most seriously, there is now a theorem that some macroscopic properties cannot be computed from the microscopic Hamiltonian even in principle: Cubitt, Perez-Garcia & Wolf (2015) proved that the spectral gap problem for a translationally invariant lattice Hamiltonian is undecidable, so that no algorithm, given the fundamental description, can determine whether the material has a gap. “Better predictions” from the fundamental model is not an unreached ideal; for some properties it is a mathematically impossible one.

quote: Reductionism is not a positive belief, but rather, a disbelief that the higher levels of simplified multilevel models are out there in the territory.
content: A claim about what is not in the territory is a positive metaphysical claim, and it is a contested one. The essay’s criterion for what is “out there” appears to be “appears in the fundamental physical description.” Dennett’s “Real Patterns” (Dennett (1991)) argues the opposite on the essay’s own grounds: a pattern is real if it supports prediction and compression that would be lost by discarding it, and the compressibility is a fact about the world, not about the compressor, since a random world would not permit it. On that criterion wings are in the territory, because the world is such that the wing description works. Ladyman and Ross’s Every Thing Must Go (2007) makes this the basis of a physics-first metaphysics that is nonetheless anti-reductionist about special-science patterns, and Schaffer (2003) points out that the existence of a fundamental level at all is an empirical bet on which the physics is not in. The essay does not argue against any of this; it defines reductionism so that it needs no argument (“not a positive belief”) and then treats the definition as the “obviously correct” hegemon the reader Matthew C. asked about. What is obviously correct is that a 747 is made of quarks and has no extra ingredient. Whether its wings are in the map or the territory is the question the essay’s definition answers by fiat.
